new_statements.quote: O tom em Tuyuka pode ser alto ou baixo. Toda palavra precisa ter pelo menos um tom alto. [...] O texto de Barnes (1996), que cito nesta subseção como caminho seminal para o estudo do tom, não fala em 'tom' propriamente dito, mas em acento – que eu estou interpretando aqui como tom, sendo o pitch alto o maior indicador do mesmo. (p. 103) [...] Porque uma raiz [A+] sempre terá stress por default e não importa qual sufixo seja associado a ela, o seu acento triunfa na hierarquia. Já raízes [A], sem acento associado, vão preservar na composição o padrão default da língua: VV́, exceto no caso de ter um sufixo [A+] (p. 104) [...] Como toda palavra tem um (e apenas um) tom alto (fn. 75, p. 77)
new_statements.translation: Tone in Tuyuka can be high or low. Every word must have at least one high tone. [...] Barnes's (1996) text, which I cite in this subsection as the seminal path for the study of tone, does not speak of 'tone' as such but of accent – which I am interpreting here as tone, high pitch being its main indicator. (p. 103) [...] Because an [A+] root will always have stress by default no matter which suffix is attached to it, its accent wins in the hierarchy. Roots [A], with no associated accent, preserve in composition the language's default pattern: VV́ [H on the last syllable], except when there is an [A+] suffix (p. 104) [...] Since every word has one (and only one) high tone (fn. 75, p. 77)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has Tuyuca with an empty rule. Vlcek supplies a full statement: culminative single H per word, lexically/morphologically placed, default on the final syllable; she reads Barnes's 'word stress' as this high pitch. Her summary of Barnes 1996 (pp. 103-104, Table 4.12 reproduced from Barnes 1996:41) is the only access we have to the 1996 article's stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tuyuca has high and low tone; every phonological word carries exactly one high tone, and Vlcek explicitly equates Barnes's 'word stress' with this high pitch (the most prominent syllable). Where the H lands is lexical-morphological: roots with a linked H ([A+]) keep it on their own (initial) syllable regardless of suffix; roots without a linked H take the language's default pattern VV́ (H on the final syllable of the word) unless an [A+] suffix contributes its own H; following Gomez-Imbert, one H per word, the first linked H wins, otherwise the first floating H, otherwise a default H is inserted, with association starting at the right edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the system is explicitly culminative (one and only one high tone per word).
new_statements.exceptions: Placement depends on morpheme class: [A+] roots keep an initial H (V́V); unmarked roots take the default final H (VV́); [A+] suffixes take the H from unmarked or [A] roots; 14 suffixes never bear word stress (summary of Barnes 1996:41, pp. 103-104). Vlcek adds that her tone analysis is preliminary and proposes a future acoustic experiment on the correlates of syllable prominence (p. 188).
new_statements.identity_note: Barnes & Silzer 1976 is based on the Colombian Tuyuca of Los Angeles on the Papurí (data from 1970, main consultant Graciliano Yepes). Vlcek 2016 documents Ʉtapinopona-Tuyuka as spoken in Brazil (São Gabriel da Cachoeira / Tiquié area, UFRJ project under Kristine Stenzel). Orjuela Salinas 2014 covers Tuyuka, Tukano and Makuna on the Colombia-Brazil border. No dialect-level differences in stress/tone are reported between these.

new_statements.relation_note: Not one of the listed works; located through the local SIL OAI cache (archive entry 18860, PDF could not be reached by automated download) and then the Rosetta Project scan on archive.org. It is the earliest primary phonology of Tuyuca and states directly that stress is a concomitant of the single high tone, whose position is lexical (any syllable), with H on the final syllable of (C)VCV disyllables. Compatible with Vlcek 2016's default VV́ pattern and with Barnes 1996 as summarised there.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two phonemic tones, high and low; the phonological word has exactly one high tone, which can fall on any syllable (so its position is lexical); stress is a concomitant feature of the high toneme. Disyllabic (C)VCV words take the high tone on the second (final) syllable, except loanwords; in words of three or more syllables the high tone may be on any syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; one high tone per word. A downstep pattern ('descenso tonal por niveles') is described for words and phrases of three or more syllables (p. 132).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (e.g. /bésa/ 'mesa', from Spanish) do not follow the final-H rule for (C)VCV disyllables; a mid allophone of low tone appears in words of three or more syllables under stated conditions.
new_statements.identity_note: Barnes & Silzer 1976 is based on the Colombian Tuyuca of Los Angeles on the Papurí (data from 1970, main consultant Graciliano Yepes). Vlcek 2016 documents Ʉtapinopona-Tuyuka as spoken in Brazil (São Gabriel da Cachoeira / Tiquié area, UFRJ project under Kristine Stenzel). new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress coincides with high pitch and by default falls on the second vowel of the word; words whose stress/high pitch falls elsewhere are marked with an acute accent in the transcribed texts (the appended Tuyuca texts carry many such acute marks, e.g. on third vowels), so the second-vowel placement is a default/majority pattern with lexically marked exceptions rather than an exceptionless rule. Note the unit is the vowel (long vowels are written double), not the syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: 'unless otherwise indicated' -- non-second-vowel stress is marked with an acute accent in the texts; no classes of exceptions are named in this work (the same author's 1976 phonology, already held by the project, names loanwords as the exceptions among (C)VCV disyllables and says the high tone may fall on any syllable in words of three or more syllables).
new_statements.identity_note: Barnes 1975 is based on fieldwork 1970-1974 in the village of Los Angeles on the Papurí River (Vaupés, Colombia), principal consultant Graciliano Yepes; Colombian Tuyuca, same variety as Barnes & Silzer 1976.

new_statements.quote: Segundo Barnes & Takagi (1976) o Tuyuka conta com dois tons fonológicos: alto e baixo. O tom baixo tem duas realizações fonéticas: um tom médio que ocorre no interior de palavras de três ou mais sílabas em que alguma sílaba contenha a vogal /i/ e siga uma sílaba com tom alto, e um tom baixo que ocorre em todos os outrsos contextos. Tom alto e acento são concomitantes. Palavras com duas sílabas (C)V.CV normalmente ocorrem com tom alto na última sílaba. Exceções a esta regra ocorrem quando a palavra é empréstimo de outra língua. Em palavras de mais de três sílabas o tom alto (e o acento) ocorre em qualquer sílaba.
new_statements.translation: According to Barnes & Takagi (1976) Tuyuka has two phonological tones: high and low. The low tone has two phonetic realizations: a mid tone that occurs inside words of three or more syllables in which some syllable contains the vowel /i/ and follows a high-toned syllable, and a low tone that occurs in all other contexts. High tone and stress are concomitant. Two-syllable (C)V.CV words normally occur with high tone on the last syllable. Exceptions to this rule occur when the word is a loan from another language. In words of more than three syllables the high tone (and the stress) occurs on any syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Restates the catalog's own source (Barnes & Takagi de Silzer 1976: two phonemic tones, H on any syllable, stress concomitant with H, disyllables H on the 2nd syllable except loans). Same type (tonal, culminative H with concomitant stress) and same disyllable placement as the catalog record and the existing B&T 1976 / Barnes 1975 statements; compatible with Vlcek 2016's pitch accent reinterpretation. Secondhand citation, not new fieldwork evidence on prosody. Minor wording difference: Orjuela writes 'palavras de mais de três sílabas' (more than three syllables) where B&T 1976 speak of words of three or more syllables; not a substantive conflict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-tone system (H vs L) reported after Barnes & Takagi 1976; stress (acento) always coincides with the high tone. In disyllabic (C)V.CV words the high tone, and hence stress, is normally on the second (final) syllable; in longer words the H/stress syllable is not positionally fixed (any syllable), i.e. lexically placed. The dissertation itself is an acoustic study of glottalization/laryngealization and adds no independent prosodic analysis; it uses 'sílaba não acentuada' (unstressed syllable) as the environment for vowel devoicing (p. 107) and notes that the vowel bearing the laryngeal suprasegment carries low tone (pp. 112-113).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords are exceptions to the disyllable final-high-tone rule (p. 99). Devoiced vowels: 'As vogais desvozeadas[fn 75] são realizações alofônicas das vogais plenas e, segundo Barnes & Takagi (1976) ocorrem em posição de V1 de sílaba não acentuada que precede outra sílaba que começa com consoante surda (i.e. C1V1.C2V2 > C1VV̥1.C2V2).' (p. 107) - devoicing only in V1 of an unstressed syllable before a voiceless onset.
new_statements.identity_note: Orjuela Salinas 2014 recorded four Tuyuka speakers (two women, two men) on the Colombian side of the Vaupés (Tuyuka located on the Tiquié, Caño Inambú and Alto Papurí, p. 56; data deposited at MPEG under ACAIPI authorization, p. 77); the prosodic statement itself is cited from Barnes & Takagi 1976 (SIL, Colombian Tuyuca) and is not dialect-specific.

readall_conflicts: No substantive disagreement between the sources actually read, only a difference in framing: Barnes & Silzer 1976 (open scan) call the system two phonemic tones with stress a concomitant of the single high tone; Barnes 1996 (known only through Vlcek's summary and the Icesi keywords) treats the same facts as accent/word stress with a three-way lexical contrast; Vlcek 2016 reinterprets Barnes's accent as tone (H vs L, exactly one H per word) and explicitly says high pitch is the main indicator of prominence. All three agree on culminativity (one H/stress per phonological word), on lexical/morphological placement (any syllable; root vs suffix class decides), and on a final-syllable default for unmarked disyllables (1976: (C)VCV words have H on the second syllable except loans; Vlcek: default VV́). Vlcek notes that the tone analysis remains preliminary and that acoustic work on the correlates of prominence is still needed. ii) states a stress rule -- stress concurrent with high pitch on the second vowel unless otherwise marked -- while Barnes & Silzer 1976 Fonología del tuyuca (already held by the project from the earlier reading, pp. 130-132) analyses the prominence as tone: each phonological word has one and only one high tone, 'El acento es un rasgo concomitante del tonema alto', tone is contrastive in (C)VV disyllables, (C)VCV disyllables take the high tone on the second syllable except loanwords, and in words of three or more syllables the high tone 'puede ocurrir en cualqu…

[...] El acento es un rasgo concomitante del tonema alto. (p. 130) [...] Las palabras de dos sílabas del modelo (C)VCV ocurren con el tono alto en la segunda sílaba, a excepción de palabras prestadas de otras lenguas. [...] En palabras de tres o más sílabas, el tono alto puede ocurrir en cualquier sílaba. (p. 131) [scanned text from the archive.org ; diacritics restored where the scanned rendered them as digits, e.g. 'fondmicos' -> 'fonémicos']
sources.locator: §5 'Los fonemas suprasegmentales', §5.1 'Tono', pp. 130-132 (deciding sentences p. 130; disyllable rule p. 131)
sources.note: Not one of the listed works; located through the local SIL OAI cache (archive entry 18860, PDF could not be reached by automated download) and then the Rosetta Project scan on archive.org. It is the earliest primary phonology of Tuyuca and states directly that stress is a concomitant of the single high tone, whose position is lexical (any syllable), with H on the final syllable of (C)VCV disyllables. Compatible with Vlcek 2016's default VV́ pattern and with Barnes 1996 as summarised there.
